cases.title: Bengaluru Metro: tax estimates, land handovers and foreign-debt support
cases.question: Did corrective procurement and land-readiness controls remove the audited sources of cost escalation before further contract and debt-service commitments?
cases.summary: A newly tabled August 2026 audit connects project estimates, contractor claims, land acquisition and international borrowing. Its observations mostly concern progress through March 2023; the missing current action-taken record is central to judging whether the problems persist.

observations.text: CAG §5.1.2 finds ₹1,098.28 crore of taxes remained in estimates for nine civil contracts although bids excluded those taxes; including quoted net premium, the audit calculated ₹1,222.40 crore higher contract prices. This is an audit calculation, not a minister-payment trail.

The audit records land-handover delays of 12–1,305 days beyond the allowed 90 days in 13 contracts. Five contractors claimed ₹98.21 crore; ₹12.19 crore had been paid on one claim at the audit snapshot. Claims and payments must remain separate.

BMRCL disclosed loans from JICA, AFD, EIB and AIIB as well as domestic institutions and bonds. The audit describes reliance on Karnataka to service external debt as of March 2023, linking project-delivery performance to the state's fiscal burden.

counterevidence.text: BMRCL replied that bidders priced independently and tender estimates were guidance. CAG disagreed because estimates informed qualification and price reasonableness; BMRCL acknowledged procurement-manual and estimation-SOP recommendations.

BMRCL attributed some land-cost increases to additional land, market-value revisions, site changes, litigation and ownership disputes. These are plausible non-corrupt explanations that require package-level testing.
The audit excludes Phases 2A and 2B and does not establish the operational condition in October 2026. A newly published old finding cannot by itself forecast a repeated failure.

cases.title: Kaleshwaram: EPC scope, supplier prices and the unresolved investigation stage
cases.question: Can package-level invoices and full installation scope reconcile the equipment-price gap identified by CAG, and what formal action has actually followed?
cases.summary: The strongest trail compares departmental estimates with information CAG obtained from BHEL. October reporting about CBI review does not establish an FIR, while August reporting raises a separate dispute about safe operation. Financing, procurement economics and dam safety must be tested independently.

observations.text: For packages 6, 8, 10 and 11, CAG Table 6.2 compares ₹7,212.34 crore estimated equipment cost with ₹1,686.59 crore charged by BHEL for its supplied scope. Those amounts cover different scopes, so their difference is not automatically a loss.

After allowing 30% for other operations, ₹85 crore per lift for common equipment and 20% overhead/profit on BHEL items, Table 6.3 identifies possible undue benefit of ₹2,684.73 crore. The estimate is explicitly conditional and disputed.

The department told CAG that contracts did not require the supplier invoices requested for other packages. This identifies a concrete documentation control to examine, without proving hidden onward payments.

The 5 October report says officials reportedly reviewed the inquiry report and legal issues following September 2025 state consent. No original CBI registration or final court outcome was inspected. The reported consent names Medigadda, Annaram and Sundilla barrages; it does not establish that the four equipment packages in this audit comparison are themselves within a registered inquiry.

counterevidence.text: Telangana's May and November 2023 responses cite tailor-made equipment, 31 major components, transportation/insurance, staged installation and testing, and argue audit allowances omitted relevant costs and profit. CAG explains why it rejected those objections; both positions remain visible.

August reporting describes an NDSA position that pumping decisions rest with the state and CWPRS findings differing between barrages. Without the originals this is a competing account, not a safety clearance or proof that prior damage was fabricated.
A reported meeting, a state consent order and an audit recommendation are different legal stages. None is a finding of individual criminal guilt.

cases.title: Chennai smart meters: repeated tenders and a ten-year service commitment
cases.question: Do the October 2026 bid documents explain changes in coverage, lifetime cost and competition after successive cancellations?
cases.summary: Latest reporting says TNPDCL has floated seven packages for about 1.7 crore consumers after prior revisions. The appropriate investigation is a versioned comparison of tender terms, bidders and future service payments; neither a cancelled bid nor an approved scheme budget establishes corruption.

observations.text: The 7 October report describes 56.85 lakh Chennai-region meters within the new programme and a separate tender for 4.72 lakh distribution-transformer meters. These are reported tender quantities, not completed installations.

The same report describes earlier tender rounds in August 2023 and March 2025, subsequent revisions and cancellations. It cites low participation and high maintenance quotes in an earlier round; the August 2026 report cites unspecified irregularity allegations.

A reported 10-year installation/maintenance service structure makes present purchase prices an incomplete measure of cost. Central support is reported as 15% of meter cost; the separate government-office programme involving PFC Consulting should not be merged with the seven consumer packages.

September reporting puts approved RDSS outlay at ₹28,731.74 crore, including ₹19,163.5 crore for smart metering. These are scheme allocations and cannot be treated as the value of October tenders or as payments.

counterevidence.text: The utility's reported explanation is that smart meters reduce delayed or incorrect readings; officials expect falling meter prices. Re-tendering can produce savings and improve competition.

The August account described approvals as prospective and gave different proposed coverage. October's later report changes the baseline, but only the original schedules can establish whether this reflects phased scope rather than impropriety.
No winning supplier, disbursement, party donation link or personal benefit is established by these sources. The record is about procurement design and verification gaps.

cases.title: Swasthya Sathi: hospital grading, insurer recoveries and scheme borrowing
cases.question: Were identified overpayments, unlevied penalties and enrolment-control weaknesses corrected after the audit reached the legislature?
cases.summary: The newly reported audit connects the state nodal agency to hospitals, insurers and borrowing costs. It supports specific recovery and control questions, while preserving the agency's explanation for family-count differences and avoiding accusations against individual beneficiaries.

observations.text: For 2018–19 through 2022–23, the audit records ₹6,882.06 crore scheme expenditure. In a 50-hospital grading sample, 31 were graded too high; ₹14.48 crore excess payments were calculated for 29 of them under assurance mode between 16 July 2022 and 31 March 2023. The other two had no financial outgo. The sample cannot be projected to all hospitals.

The audit says ₹31.33 crore penalties were not imposed on National, Oriental and United India Insurance companies for claims delays under the reviewed agreements. It separately identifies ₹9.78 crore refunds due from National Insurance and Bajaj Allianz. These are different obligations, not one cash loss.

The nodal agency paid ₹10.85 crore interest on ₹721.95 crore loans during 2020–22, according to §1.9.2. Budget sufficiency and health-service delivery therefore need to be studied alongside provider claims.
Audit records 2.43 crore enrolled families against 2.21 crore ration-card families at different 2023 dates. This is a reconciliation trigger, not a count of fake beneficiaries.

counterevidence.text: The nodal agency cited population growth, family splitting and ongoing Aadhaar mapping/data sanitisation. Different database dates and definitions may explain part of the gap.
The audit also records actual corrective activity: February–March 2023 post-discharge audits imposed ₹11.78 crore penalties and recovered ₹8.36 crore at that snapshot.

Public super-speciality hospitals were themselves under-graded in the audit, showing a system-wide grading problem rather than a simple universal private-hospital preference. Newer claims and recovery records have not been inspected.

cases.title: Odisha mineral welfare: village eligibility, police vehicles and returned funds
cases.question: Can each questioned DMF allocation be reconciled to an eligible affected population, lawful purpose, sanction, payment and any repayment?
cases.summary: September reporting on a newly tabled CAG audit links mining-derived welfare funds to stadium and police-vehicle expenditure while some directly affected villages received no DMF project. The original audit remains a priority gap; Bhubaneswar is the oversight location, not the location of all works.

observations.text: Reporting attributes to CAG a ₹136.77 crore Sundargarh DMF sanction for the Rourkela hockey stadium, questioned against PMKKKY purposes. The Indian Express calls this a sanction; other reports describe expenditure, so the actual disbursement stage remains to be reconciled.

The Indian Express reports ₹4.63 crore released to Rourkela SP for 25 patrolling vehicles, subsequently re-deposited without ₹22.53 lakh interest. Return of principal is material counterevidence against portraying the entire release as retained money.

Hindustan Times reports ₹983.32 crore expenditure in 976 non-affected villages in Keonjhar and Sundargarh, while 488 directly affected villages had no DMF-funded project during 2015–24. The classifications and overlapping totals require original records.
The reported funding source is statutory contributions by mining leaseholders. This does not establish that a specific mining company controlled any beneficiary decision or received the money back.

counterevidence.text: The police-vehicle principal was reportedly re-deposited, so the remaining issue includes interest, authority and opportunity cost rather than an assumed unrecovered ₹4.63 crore.
BJD leaders told the Indian Express they would respond after reading the report. That is a pending response, not an admission; no subsequent response or adjudication was established in this search.
An asset may have public value while its funding source is impermissible. Neither construction of a stadium nor association with a police office proves private enrichment.

cases.title: KIIFB: follow publicity invoices through each intermediary
cases.question: Can the missing lower-tier invoices and vendor-selection record reconcile the publicity cost to actual end suppliers, services and authorised project purposes?
cases.summary: The original FY2025–26 accounts create a concrete invoice-chain investigation. A qualified audit opinion concerns ₹79.977 crore publicity documentation; separate ₹102.8855 crore programme costs are emphasis matters without modified opinions. These different findings must not be collapsed into one corruption total.

observations.text: Standalone auditor pp.67–68 states ₹7,997.70 lakh (₹79.977 crore) was allocated to project promotion through outsourced media arrangements and classified as direct project cost. Vendor-selection documentation did not sufficiently establish the process to the auditor.

First-level invoices were available for ₹6,238.88 lakh, but the required media-house second-level invoices were not produced. For another ₹744.53 lakh, first- and second-level invoices were produced but the next provider's invoice was absent. These are distinct documentation gaps, not proof that all services were fictitious.

₹1,985.40 lakh incurred before 13 February 2026 was ratified afterward; ₹6,012.29 lakh followed the board's sanction up to 1% of project cost. The auditor acknowledged that framework while recommending activity budgets, pre-approvals and end-use certification. The two components differ by ₹0.01 lakh from the stated total; no adverse inference is made from rounding.

Auditor p.71 separately draws attention to ₹614.21 lakh and ₹9,644.34 lakh infrastructure-related programme costs under government orders, expressly without modifying its opinion for those matters. October reporting identifies them as 'CM With Me' and 'Ente Keralam'.

The annual report lists commercial and public-sector banking relationships, but the inspected publicity passage does not trace a particular loan drawdown to these invoices. A loan-to-publicity cash lineage remains unproven.

counterevidence.text: Management told the auditor that vendor selection followed due process and rates were competitive. The auditor says evidence of the amount spent was verified and relied on Media Cell receipt authentication and CEO approval; missing next-tier bills must not be rewritten as no evidence at all.

KIIFB told the news outlet publicity supports brand credibility needed to raise market funds. Former vice-chair K N Balagopal said spending was within the mandate while also saying he had not seen the audit report.

The separate programme costs have government-order authority and unmodified emphasis treatment. An audit qualification is a limit on assurance for specified matters, not a criminal verdict or proof of the ₹79.977 crore being stolen.

cases.title: HAL–GE: contract value, engine shipments and aircraft acceptance
cases.question: Will engine supply and certification milestones support the public delivery commitments, and are contractual delay remedies actually recovered?
cases.summary: Original contract announcements and current named responses support a foreign-supplier dependency graph. The measurable concern is delivery and enforcement, with no evidence here of an illicit arms-dealing or personal-payment route.

observations.text: GE's August 2021 announcement values the 99-engine-and-support order at $716 million with overall delivery commitment by 2029. This is the first programme's engine contract, not proof of funds disbursed or an immediate deadline for all 99 engines.

The second MoD–HAL contract, announced September 25 2025, covers 97 aircraft at over ₹62,370 crore excluding taxes, with deliveries beginning 2027–28 over six years. It is distinct from the first 83-aircraft programme.

On October 7 2026, reporting quotes GE announcing four September shipments and describes a 14-engine tally. Shipping, HAL receipt, aircraft certification and IAF acceptance are separate milestones and must be recorded separately.

The same report says HAL is imposing liquidated damages and expects 22 engines by year-end. Assessment, recovery and any waiver were not independently verified; neither damages nor supplier nationality establishes corruption.

counterevidence.text: HAL CMD Ravi K's September interview describes remaining radar/software standard-confirmation tests, not an engine-only explanation. His statement of ten engines received was a September snapshot, not a contradiction to later shipments.
GE's reported four-engine shipment indicates progress. A programme may miss near-term milestones while still being within the overall 2029 commitment for the original engine order.
The official second-tranche delivery start is 2027–28. It would be incorrect to label those 97 aircraft overdue in October 2026.
